slides.summary: This introductory lecture on scripting languages is presented by Tim Van de Cruys for the Faculty of Arts. The session, identified as Lecture 1, took place on Wednesday, 23 September 2026.

slides.title: Introduction
slides.summary: This introductory course teaches programming using Python to collect, process, and analyze humanities data such as text, tables, and web sources. It assumes no prior experience while fostering an algorithmic way of thinking applicable across languages. The primary objective is practical application: writing scripts to effectively get things done in research contexts.

slides.title: Scripting languages?
slides.summary: Scripting languages differ from traditional programming languages by executing code on the fly without prior compilation, though this distinction is diminishing due to modern hardware speed. This course adopts a hands-on scripting approach where ease of development and automating specific tasks, such as text processing for digital humanities, are prioritized over program efficiency. The primary goal is to quickly process large-scale data and automate repetitive tasks that would be tedious to perform manually.

slides.title: Scripting languages = Python
slides.summary: The course primarily focuses on learning Python, a scripting language chosen for its ease and intuitive nature. Its code is designed to be easily understandable, resembling plain English. Additionally, Python offers access to many useful libraries, particularly those beneficial for data science applications.

slides.title: Who is in the room?
slides.summary: This course accommodates students from diverse backgrounds, including Digital Humanities and Sociology (6 ECTS) or Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (4 ECTS). Lectures begin at a zero-experience level for beginners, while those with prior programming skills can access more challenging exercises in practical sessions. Both versions share the same lectures and exam, though the 6 ECTS track includes an additional project component.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.summary: The course learning goals combine theoretical foundations in computational thinking and programming language concepts with a primary emphasis on practical Python skills. Students will develop competencies in text processing, data analysis, visualization, and data collection while mastering researcher workflows like command-line usage and script execution. Additionally, the curriculum focuses on reading, evaluating, and debugging code, including that generated by AI tools, supported by dedicated practical sessions for hands-on application.

slides.title: Format of the course
slides.summary: The course consists of 12 on-campus lectures with recordings posted on Toledo at the end of the term. Code-along notebooks are published before each class, and every lecture except the first includes a practical session on Wednesdays from 4pm to 6pm. These sessions feature tiered exercises (warm-up, core, challenge) with student assistance available during the time and solutions released afterwards.

slides.title: Practical information
slides.summary: Course materials, including slides, notebooks, reading material, and exercises, are available online via the Toledo platform. Students can ask questions through the course forum on Toledo or during Q&A sessions in lectures and practicals. It is essential to regularly check the Toledo course page for updates.

slides.title: Content of the course
slides.summary: This course covers Python fundamentals including values, variables, strings, lists, conditions, loops, functions, and dictionaries. It progresses to file handling, command line usage, modules, error management, object-oriented programming, text processing, regular expressions, and tabular data analysis with pandas. The curriculum concludes with web data collection, Digital Humanities applications, and coding with AI tools.

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.summary: The 4 ECTS version is evaluated solely by a final exam, while the 6 ECTS version combines a final exam (two-thirds) with an independent project applying course techniques to a chosen dataset (one-third). The full project brief appears in lecture 5. Additionally, two ungraded assignments and a mock exam are strongly recommended for self-assessment but do not count toward the final grade.

slides.title: The exam
slides.summary: The course concludes with a computer-based exam held on campus in January, where students submit programming exercises as notebooks. These tasks assess practical skills including writing, reading, explaining, and fixing code, mirroring the content of practical sessions. While specific formats and rules regarding AI tool usage will be announced during the semester, the professor emphasizes that understanding code is essential to effectively control and take responsibility for any AI-generated solutions.

slides.title: Computers for DH research?
slides.summary: Computers enable Digital Humanities research by automating tedious tasks, amplifying analysis beyond human capacity, and ensuring reproducibility through shared data and code. Algorithms consistently identify patterns in large corpora without fatigue, allowing researchers to distribute their scripts so others can verify results or build upon them. This approach supports practical applications like text processing, exploratory data analysis, and collecting data from the internet.

slides.title: Programming for DH research?
slides.summary: To process data automatically in Digital Humanities research, scholars can either use existing tools or create custom scripts. While existing tools offer immediate functionality, they are limited to predefined features and often make repeating action sequences difficult. Conversely, writing one's own programs requires a higher initial investment but provides endless opportunities for automation and ensures that research results are reproducible.

slides.title: Learning to program in 2026
slides.summary: Although large language models can generate Python code, learning programming remains essential to specify needs precisely, judge correctness, and debug failures on specific data. Students must understand the underlying logic to take responsibility for results, as generated code often appears correct but contains subtle errors. Consequently, the advice for the first weeks is to type code manually while using AI tools solely for explanation rather than solution generation.

slides.title: Python is a language
slides.summary: Python is a scripting language characterized by three core components: words, syntax, and semantics. Words are the primitive constructs or basic building blocks used to form larger units. Syntax defines the rules stipulating how these words combine, while semantics represents the meaning derived from both the words and their specific combination according to syntactic rules.

slides.title: Words
slides.summary: In the context of scripting languages like Python, "words" encompass not only textual identifiers but also numerical values and simple arithmetic operators such as addition (+), subtraction (-), and multiplication (*). This slide establishes that these fundamental elements are treated as basic units or tokens within the language's structure.

slides.title: Words
slides.summary: Python programming relies on a limited set of English words known as keywords, such as "while," alongside numbers and simple operators like plus, minus, and multiplication. Additionally, Python allows users to invent their own custom words called variables, which hold specific meaning defined by the programmer. Together, these elements constitute the fundamental vocabulary used to construct scripts in this language.

slides.title: Syntax
slides.summary: In the context of scripting languages, syntax refers to the rules that determine whether an expression is structurally correct. Some expressions are syntactically valid, meaning they adhere to these rules, while others are not. This distinction establishes the fundamental requirement for code to be recognized as properly formed before it can be executed or evaluated.

slides.title: Syntax
slides.summary: Syntax defines the rules determining whether expressions are valid within a language. The slide illustrates this using English: "the dog chases the cat" is syntactically valid because it correctly arranges a subject, verb, and object. In contrast, jumbled phrases like "cat library the sleep bottle" violate these structural rules and are therefore invalid.

slides.title: Syntax
slides.summary: Syntax in English distinguishes between expressions that are structurally valid and those that are not. For instance, "the dog chases the cat" is syntactically valid, whereas "cat library the sleep bottle" is not. This slide illustrates how word order determines whether a sequence of words forms a grammatically correct sentence.

slides.title: Syntax
slides.summary: Syntax defines the structural rules a programming language requires for valid expressions. In Python, `2.5 * 14` is syntactically valid and executes successfully, whereas `"welcome" 2.5 in` triggers a syntax error because it violates these rules. Just as nonsensical word sequences like "cat library the sleep bottle" cannot be parsed in English, code must strictly follow syntactic conventions before its meaning, or semantics, can be evaluated.

slides.title: Syntax
slides.summary: In Python, expressions must adhere to specific syntactic rules to be valid and interpretable by the language. The expression `2.5 * 14` is syntactically valid because it correctly combines numbers with a multiplication operator. Conversely, `"welcome" 2.5 in` is not syntactically valid as it lacks proper constituents and fails to follow Python's structural rules, preventing interpretation.

slides.title: Semantics
slides.summary: Semantics concerns the meaning of expressions within a language. While certain expressions may be syntactically valid, they can still be non-sensical if they lack logical meaning. This distinction highlights that correct structure does not guarantee meaningful content in scripting languages.

slides.title: Semantics
slides.summary: Semantics refers to the meaning of expressions constructed using syntactic rules. While some phrases like "the man reads the newspaper" are both syntactically valid and meaningful, others like "the lightbulb sings a banana" follow grammatical structure yet remain nonsensical due to illogical subject-verb-object relationships. This distinction between syntactic validity and semantic sense applies equally to English and Python programming languages.

slides.title: Semantics
slides.summary: Semantics distinguishes between expressions that are syntactically valid yet non-sensical. The phrase "the man reads the newspaper" is semantically felicitous, whereas "the lightbulb sings a banana" is semantically anomalous despite being grammatically correct. This contrast illustrates how meaning constraints operate independently of syntactic structure in English.

slides.title: Semantics
slides.summary: Semantics in Python distinguishes between syntactically valid expressions that are meaningful versus those that are nonsensical. While `2 + 5` is valid and executes correctly, `"welcome" + 1` adheres to syntax rules but fails semantically because Python cannot combine a string and an integer. This type mismatch triggers an error, illustrating that correct structure does not guarantee logical meaning or successful execution.

slides.title: Semantics
slides.summary: Semantics distinguishes between expressions that are syntactically valid but non-sensical. In Python, the expression `2 + 5` is semantically felicitous because it makes logical sense, whereas `"welcome" + 1` is semantically anomalous despite being syntactically correct. This slide illustrates how certain operations fail to produce meaningful results even when they follow proper grammatical rules.

slides.title: Semantics (bis)
slides.summary: The sentence "I saw the man with the telescope" illustrates semantic ambiguity in English, where the phrase "with the telescope" can modify either the noun (the man possesses it) or the verb (the observer uses it). While humans typically infer a single intended meaning, programming languages face similar challenges where expressions possess one specific meaning that may differ from the programmer's intent. This concept is exemplified by arithmetic expressions like "2 plus 5 times 10," highlighting the critical need for precise semantic definitions in code.

slides.title: Semantics (bis)
slides.summary: In Python, every expression possesses exactly one single meaning. However, this definitive meaning may differ from what the programmer originally intended when writing the code. This distinction highlights that while the language's interpretation is unambiguous, it does not guarantee alignment with the developer's expectations.

slides.title: Semantics (bis)
slides.summary: In Python, expressions possess a single, unambiguous meaning determined by strict evaluation rules, which may differ from a programmer's intent. For instance, `2 + 5 * 10` evaluates to 52 because multiplication precedes addition, whereas a human might incorrectly expect 70 by summing first. Without explicit brackets, expressions that appear ambiguous to humans are resolved definitively by the computer's precedence rules.

slides.title: Semantics (bis)
slides.summary: In Python, expressions possess a single, unambiguous meaning defined by the language semantics. However, this precise meaning may differ from what the programmer originally intended when writing the code. The slide illustrates this concept with the expression `(2 + 5) * 10`, highlighting the distinction between syntactic correctness and semantic expectation in scripting languages.

slides.title: Semantics (bis)
slides.summary: In Python, expressions possess a single, unambiguous meaning defined by the language rules. However, this precise semantic meaning may differ from what the programmer originally intended when writing the code. The slide illustrates this concept using the arithmetic expression "2 + (5 * 10)" to highlight how scripting languages interpret operations strictly according to their defined semantics.

slides.title: Learning a language
slides.summary: Learning Python mirrors learning a spoken language, requiring practice and the acceptance of mistakes as essential for progress. Syntactic errors are common but easily identified by Python's explicit error messages, while significant semantic anomalies like type errors are also flagged. However, subtle semantic differences or ambiguity may produce no error message yet cause unexpected behaviors such as crashes, infinite loops, or incorrect results because the code's meaning differs from the programmer's intent.

slides.title: Python script
slides.summary: A Python script is a sequence of definitions and commands written one after another. Definitions are evaluated by the language for later use, while commands (statements) instruct the interpreter to execute specific actions. These scripts can either be typed directly into a shell or stored in a file that is read into the shell for evaluation.

slides.title: Objects
slides.summary: In Python, scripts manipulate data objects where each object's type defines the specific operations permissible on it, analogous to how a banana (fruit) can be eaten or Kim (human) can walk. Objects are categorized as either scalar, which cannot be subdivided like a whole number, or non-scalar, which possess an internal structure that allows access to individual elements, such as items within a list.

slides.title: How to run Python code?
slides.summary: Running Python code involves three primary methods: scripting, interactive shells, and notebooks. The scripting approach follows a two-step process where you write and save code in a file, then execute it with a Python interpreter, repeating this cycle to solve errors. Alternatively, an interactive shell allows typing commands directly for immediate execution, while notebooks provide the most interactive experience by combining explanatory text, code, and results within a web browser interface like Google Colab.

slides.title: Installing Python
slides.summary: The professor recommends installing the Anaconda distribution from anaconda.com rather than the main Python release, which can be cumbersome for beginners. Anaconda is a user-friendly option suitable for data science and machine learning that simplifies package management and includes Jupyter Notebook for practical sessions. The download page automatically detects your operating system to provide the correct installer for Windows, macOS, or Linux.

slides.title: Reference material
slides.summary: The recommended reference material is "Python for Everybody" by Charles Severance, available at py4e.com. This resource focuses on Python for data processing and includes a book, additional videos, and exercises under a Creative Commons license. It serves as the primary supplementary text for this course module on scripting languages.
